metadata.notes:
English abstract

This article analyzes the impact of disinformation and fake news circulating on social networks on public moral security. The fast-paced and widely accessible information space of social networks facilitates the rapid spread of false information. This situation reduces public trust, intensifies political and social divisions, and negatively affects public health and psychological stability during emergencies such as pandemics.

Русская аннотация

В статье анализируется влияние дезинформации и фейковых новостей, распространяемых в социальных сетях, на общественную нравственную безопасность. Быстрое и широкое распространение информации в социальных сетях способствует стремительному распространению ложных сведений. Эта ситуация снижает общественное доверие, усиливает политические и социальные расколы, а также негативно влияет на общественное здоровье и психологическую устойчивость в чрезвычайных ситуациях, таких как пандемии.

metadata.title: IMPROVING THE PHYSICAL TRAINING OF SCHOOL STUDENTS USING ATHLETIC TOOLS
metadata.description: Annotatsion.This work highlights the theoretical and methodological foundations for developing speed and speed-strength qualities in schoolchildren during physical education classes through short-distance running. The effectiveness of general and special exercises aimed at developing speed, running methods, and age-appropriate training tools was analyzed. Additionally, the significance of modern methods used in physical education classes in enhancing students' physical fitness and improving motor skills is revealed.

metadata.title: Fab26 – Reimagine the Future. Fab26 Research Papers Stream
metadata.description:
FAB26 marked the 25th anniversary of the Fab Lab phenomenon, its network and movement. The conference was as much looking back at that legacy as looking forward to the next 25 years. The fifteen papers in this year's research stream stand at that watershed, building on the past and for the future. The papers fall into three clusters, presented across three sessions: Teaching & Learning, Making with Communities, and Sustaining and Scaling.

Teaching & Learning: From First Stitch to Education 5.0 — pedagogy, tools, and AI across the learner's journey — opens with a small piece of hardware: Leirado et al. develop sew:bit, an open-source expansion board that makes the BBC micro:bit work for e-textiles much as the LilyPad once did for Arduino. LaPrade proposes The Armature, a community-first framework carrying middle-school makers at a Title I school in Cleveland toward a professional CAD credential. Yalçın reports seven years of a K-12 FabLab in Istanbul in which students become co-authors of peer-reviewed HCI research. Llàcer Caro and Muñoz Zanón ask what critical thinking means once generative AI is ubiquitous, and offer a toolkit built on deliberate friction. Hernández-Montoya and Miranda close the session with an AI-mediated model joining remote, physical, and mobile Fab Labs at a Costa Rican distance university.

Making with Communities: From Visiting to Becoming Infrastructure — resilience and sustainability transitions on the ground — moves outward. Liu and Liao use a seven-day Fab City Challenge to read Shenzhen's Nantou Ancient City through fabrication. Espinoza Gómez et al. ask honestly what it would take to evaluate an itinerant digital fabrication programme in rural Peru, having first run one without a baseline. de Castro Lacerda and Tenório Ramalho de Abreu describe a participatory method for textile waste with women upcycling decommissioned bus-driver uniforms in Brasília. Regina et al. explore village-scale green hydrogen in coastal Bali through five co-designed interventions, built on the existing governance of the Balinese banjar. Anaya Hernández asks whether maker networks actually hold the data needed to be activated in a disaster, and finds the answer uneven.

Sustaining and Scaling: From One Workshop to the Full Stack — governance, stakeholders, and measurement of fab initiatives — turns to what makes any of this last. Stadlmann and Holzinger treat maker workshops for children as multi-stakeholder services and find that stakeholders do not agree on what those services are for. Doyo draws on ten years of a Japanese university FabLab to argue that openness is a three-layer achievement of place, governance, and participatory mediation. León Lucano proposes Fab Lab venture studios as a university investment framework for Peru. Freundt et al. report a national faculty-development programme reaching 27 public technical institutes. Vivanco closes with the Fab City Full Stack Metrics Framework, an attempt to make local activity measurable without severing it from the systems it sits in.

Twenty-nine papers were submitted to this year's stream. The stream's policy is double-blind peer review, with each paper receiving at least two reviews; on that basis fourteen were accepted and one was rerouted as a preprint. Their thirty-one authors work in twenty-two institutions across thirteen countries. Each paper is deposited separately and carries its own DOI, listed in the contents that follow; this volume gathers their abstracts and is the citable record of the stream as a whole. The research papers stream has run since Fab8 in Wellington in 2012, a history set out in Troxler, Fab Lab Research Papers. From Experiment to Expression (10.5281/zenodo.1344101); the most recent volume was Fab25 Czechia – Bridge the Gap (10.5281/zenodo.16789442).

The editors thank the reviewers, who each carried six to eight papers: Serena Cangiano, Pablo C. Herrera, Jan Peuckert, Ivan Sanchez Milara, Alessandra Schmidt, Jessica Stanley, Sarina Till, and Liz Whitewolf.

metadata.title: Comparative Study of Warm Mix vs Hot Mix Asphalt Performance
metadata.description: This research paper presents a comprehensive comparative analysis of Warm Mix Asphalt (WMA) and Hot Mix Asphalt (HMA) technologies for flexible pavement applications. Hot Mix Asphalt has served as the industry standard for road construction for decades, prized for its mechanical strength and durability. However, the substantial environmental footprint of HMA production requiring temperatures of 150–170°C has prompted the development of WMA, which reduces production and compaction temperatures by 20–40°C through the use of additives such as Sasobit or water-foaming techniques. This study evaluates both mix types using the Marshall Mix Design methodology, with laboratory specimens prepared at their respective mixing and compaction temperatures. A battery of standardized tests including Marshall Stability, Indirect Tensile Strength (ITS), Moisture Susceptibility (TSR), Wheel Tracking, and RTFO Aging  was conducted under identical conditions. Emissions and energy data were also analysed to quantify environmental benefits. Results indicate that WMA with 1.5% Sasobit additive achieves mechanical performance comparable to HMA: Marshall Stability of 11.5 kN vs. 12.0 kN, ITS of 620 kPa vs. 650 kPa, and TSR values above 80% for both mixes. WMA demonstrated approximately 30% reduction in fuel consumption and CO2 emissions, 20% reduction in NOx, and 50% reduction in VOCs. Rutting resistance was marginally lower in WMA (4.0 mm vs. 3.5 mm rut depth) but remained within acceptable limits. These findings support the adoption of WMA as a technically viable, environmentally superior, and economically competitive alternative to conventional HMA.

metadata.title: Desa Hidrogen Hijau: A Dual-Track Methodology for Village-Scale Energy Transition Integrating Social and Technical Development in Coastal Bali
metadata.description: Energy-transition research lacks methods to integrate technical development with community social and cultural realities. Technology-first interventions in the Global South often fail socially, yet literature offers no tested model for structuring recursive exchanges between community insights and engineering. This paper tests a dual-track methodology—parallel Community and Technology Development workstreams coupled by structured feedback loops—within a village-scale "sandbox." Here, energy systems are co-developed with residents, academic, enterprise, and government actors, orchestrated by an embedded fab lab. Evaluating a two-year (2023–2025) participatory action-research study of the Desa Hidrogen Hijau (Green Hydrogen Village) project in Serangan, Bali, we ground the work in multiscalar village reading, commons governance, and appropriate-technology principles. Across five co-developed interventions, parallel development surfaced design parameters absent from prior specifications. We demonstrate that the Balinese banjar, anchored by the bale banjar, functions as both governance infrastructure and a replicable substrate, proving energy transition can be built on existing culture, not imposed as standalone hardware. Finally, we document an enthusiasm-to-maintenance gap, highlighting the need for a third track of institutional embedding.

metadata.title: Automation of Reporting Tasks and Its Impact on Bandwidth for Customer Experience Managers
metadata.description: Organizations increasingly automate reporting to reduce the manual effort of collecting, verifying, and circulating operational data, a burden that falls heavily on Customer Experience (CX) managers in Software-as-a-Service firms. This study examines whether employee perceptions of automation across five dimensions - Productivity/Time Savings, Ease of Use, Speed & Timeliness, Quality & Error Reduction, and Trust & Satisfaction - predict their overall perception that automation improves operational efficiency and releases bandwidth for higher-value work. Data were collected from 84 working professionals using a 20-item, five-point Likert-scale questionnaire administered through Google Forms. The instrument demonstrated excellent reliability (Cronbach's alpha = 0.918). Descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and multiple linear regression were used for analysis, with regression assumptions (normality, multicollinearity, homoscedasticity, autocorrelation) verified. All five constructs correlated positively and significantly with the overall outcome (r = 0.498-0.646), and together explained 50.3% of its variance (R² = 0.503). Speed & Timeliness (β = 0.526), Productivity/Time Savings (β = 0.450), and Ease of Use (β = 0.413) emerged as the strongest predictors. Findings suggest that organizations seeking to maximize perceived bandwidth release should prioritize automating high-frequency, time-consuming tasks and keep interfaces simple, rather than investing primarily in trust-building initiatives.
keywords: reporting automation, customer experience management, operational efficiency, bandwidth release, technology acceptance, business intelligence.

dates.description: More recently, automation, whether through scripting tools, process-flow automation, artificial intelligence, or business intelligence (BI) platforms, has begun to reshape how reports are generated. These technologies collect and present data both quickly and reliably. By automating report generation, organizations stand to gain considerably in terms of efficiency, since the process saves time and effort, improves the accuracy of the output, and speeds up how quickly information reaches decision-makers. This is especially relevant for Software-as-a-Service (SaaS) companies, many of which must handle substantial volumes of data on an ongoing basis. These companies routinely track subscription metrics, customer behavior, service operations, support requests, renewals, and refunds, all of which fall under the broader umbrella of key performance indicators (KPIs). Given that Customer Experience (CX) managers are typically the ones responsible for this kind of analysis, manually compiling reports becomes both cumbersome and time-intensive, ultimately preventing organizations from reaching their desired levels of efficiency.

metadata.title: UPPER RESPIRATORY TRACT INFECTION: TREATMENT GUIDELINES
metadata.description: Upper respiratory tract infections (URTIs) are among the most common infectious diseases worldwide and represent a significant cause of morbidity across all age groups. URTIs affect structures including the nasal cavities, sinuses, pharynx, and larynx. These infections are mainly viral in origin, though bacterial pathogens may contribute to complications or secondary infections. URTIs result in substantial healthcare utilization, absenteeism from work and school, and increased economic burden. Risk factors include environmental pollution, overcrowding, smoking, and poor nutritional status. Management primarily focuses on symptomatic treatment, preventive strategies, and rational antibiotic use to prevent resistance. This review summarizes the epidemiology, etiology, pathophysiology, clinical features, diagnosis, management, and preventive measures of URTIs.
